clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia caused by heterozygous KCND3 variants; SCA19 and SCA22 were mapped separately but are the same allelic disorder.
KCND3 encodes the Kv4.3 voltage-gated potassium channel alpha subunit that carries the transient A-type outward current shaping Purkinje neuron firing.
Gait and limb ataxia with dysarthria are the core features, typically evolving over years.
Cognitive impairment and executive dysfunction are relatively common and can help distinguish it from purely motor cerebellar syndromes.
Additional signs include postural/action tremor, myoclonus, hyporeflexia and, in some pedigrees, a mild peripheral sensory neuropathy.
Age of onset is wide (childhood to late adulthood) with marked intrafamilial variability.
MRI usually shows cerebellar (predominantly vermian) atrophy with relative brainstem sparing, but can appear normal early.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA19 is caused by pathogenic variants in KCND3, which encodes the pore-forming alpha subunit of the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv4.3. This channel generates the fast transient (A-type) outward potassium current that regulates dendritic excitability, back-propagating action potentials and repetitive firing of cerebellar Purkinje cells. Missense and small in-frame variants impair trafficking of the channel to the plasma membrane and/or alter its gating, reducing surface A-type current; mutant subunits also exert a dominant-negative effect by co-assembling with wild-type subunits and retaining them within the endoplasmic reticulum. The resulting disturbance of Purkinje cell firing and intracellular calcium handling drives progressive Purkinje cell dysfunction and degeneration, producing the cerebellar phenotype and, in some individuals, the associated cognitive and peripheral nerve features.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal dominant SCAs, especially channelopathies (SCA6 due to CACNA1A; SCA13 due to KCNC3)
SCA14 (PRKCG) and other conventional-mutation dominant ataxias
Polyglutamine SCAs with cognitive involvement (SCA17, dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy)
Acquired cerebellar ataxia (alcohol, anticonvulsant toxicity, immune-mediated) and multiple system atrophy, cerebellar type
additionalInvestigations: KCND3 sequencing, ideally within a next-generation hereditary ataxia gene panel
Brain MRI to document cerebellar/vermian atrophy and exclude structural mimics
Repeat-expansion testing to exclude common polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias
Nerve conduction studies where a peripheral neuropathy is suspected
Neuropsychometric assessment for cognitive and executive dysfunction
Detailed family history with segregation and cascade genetic testing
redFlags: Rapid or subacute progression suggesting an acquired, toxic or paraneoplastic cause rather than SCA19
Prominent early autonomic or pyramidal/brainstem features pointing to multiple system atrophy
Emerging cognitive decline requiring formal assessment and support
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive with ambulation preserved for many years and a life expectancy that is often near-normal. Disability accrues gradually and associated cognitive involvement may affect independence.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal MRI excludes the diagnosis early in the disease course
Overlooking cognitive impairment as part of the phenotype and attributing it to an unrelated condition
Not recognising that SCA19 and SCA22 are the same KCND3 disorder, which causes confusion when reviewing the literature
Relying only on repeat-expansion panels, which miss this conventional (non-expansion) mutation
